sections.b: Paul takes the language of the altar and applies it to ordinary life: believers are to place their bodies before God as a sacrifice that is alive, holy and welcome to God, which he calls "sensible worship." The animal on the altar was killed; this sacrifice goes on living. Paul uses the same idea of his own work: he does a priest's work for the good news, and the Gentiles who believe are the offering (Romans 15:16, echoing Isaiah 66:20). Hebrews 13:15-16 and 1 Peter 2:5 speak of praise and good deeds as sacrifices in the same way.

The phrase logikē latreia has been rendered "reasonable service," "spiritual worship" and "rational worship." Paul puts worship in the whole life of the believer. The Orthodox liturgy of St John Chrysostom calls the Eucharistic offering a "reasonable service," from this verse. In 16:16 the "holy kiss" is another early worship practice, now the kiss of peace in the Catholic, Orthodox and other liturgies.

Paul lists seven gifts: prophecy, service, teaching, encouragement, giving, leading and showing mercy. Each is to be used for the body: prophecy "in line with the proportion of faith," giving "with generosity," mercy "with cheerfulness." The list has no tongues or miracles, and differs from the lists in 1 Corinthians 12 and Ephesians 4:11. The gifts come by grace and are given for the common good, and they belong to the "one body" with many parts.

"Chase after hospitality to strangers," Paul writes, and he asks the Romans to welcome Phoebe, who had been a patron to many. Traveling believers, couriers and teachers depended on the homes of other believers, and host households such as those of Prisca and Aquila (16:5) and Gaius (16:23) made the church work. The word philoxenia is literally "love of strangers."

sections.h: Do not repay evil for evil (Romans 12:14-21)
sections.b: Paul tells the Romans to bless persecutors, to repay no one evil for evil, to keep the peace so far as they can, and to leave vengeance to God. He quotes Deuteronomy 32:35 and Proverbs 25:21-22 (feed your hungry enemy; this will "heap coals of fire" on his head) and ends: "Do not be defeated by evil. Defeat evil with good." The language echoes Jesus' teaching on loving enemies (Matthew 5:44; Luke 6:28). Right after, he says the ruler "does not carry the sword for no reason" (13:4), and Christians have drawn different conclusions about force; see the topic on the church and the ruler.

Paul tells the Romans not to take revenge but "make room for the anger," which nearly all take as God's anger at the last judgment, quoting a line from the Song of Moses in Paul's own form: "Vengeance is mine. I will pay back, says the Lord." In 13:4 the ruler too is "an avenger to carry out anger" on the wrongdoer. Paul's use of "anger" in Romans runs from 1:18 (God's anger revealed) to 12:19, where the believer is told to leave it to God.

Paul says the only debt to leave outstanding is the debt of love. The commands against adultery, murder, theft and coveting, and every other command, are "all gathered up" in Leviticus 19:18, "You are to love your neighbor as yourself," and "love is the law fulfilled." Jesus (Mark 12:31), Paul (Galatians 5:14) and James (James 2:8) each give this verse the same place. Jewish teachers also named it a great principle of the Torah (Rabbi Akiva; compare Hillel).

Paul tells the Roman believers to submit to the governing authorities, which God has set in place and which are "God's servant, there for your good," to pay taxes and give respect and honor. He wrote at the start of Nero's reign, with the memory of Claudius' expulsion of the Jews and anger at tax collectors in the air. The passage has been read as a general rule, as advice for one moment and as a limit on rulers; it has been used to defend rulers and to resist them. Peter in Acts 5:29 gives a limit: "Obeying God has to come before obeying people." The card at Romans 13 gives what the churches teach.

The last chapters of Romans show the city that Paul writes to: Jewish and Gentile believers in at least five house groups, many with the names of slaves and freed people, some in the households of Aristobulus and Narcissus (16:10-11); Prisca and Aquila, back after the Claudian expulsion (16:3-5; Acts 18:2); a tax system under strain (13:6-7; Tacitus, Annals 13.50-51); and Paul's plan to come through on his way to Spain (15:24, 28). Whether Peter had been in Rome by then is not stated in the letter.

sections.h: Romans 14: nothing is common in itself
sections.b: Paul says he is "convinced in the Lord Jesus" that nothing is common in itself, but he asks the strong to give up what offends the weak. The weak eat only vegetables (14:2) and the strong eat everything, but he never says that Jews must stop keeping the food laws of Leviticus 11. Christians have read this as the end of those laws for believers (most traditions), as a freedom with limits, or as a text about Gentile food, not Torah law (some readers within the "Paul within Judaism" view). See the card for what the churches teach. Mark 7:19 and Acts 10:15 are the nearest parallels.

Paul writes that one person judges one day above another, and another judges every day alike, and each should be fully sure. He does not name the Sabbath, though it is the likeliest of the days in mind, with fast days and festivals. The passage is used on every side of the Christian discussion of the Sabbath: as showing the Sabbath is not binding, as showing it is a matter of conscience, or as speaking of other days than the weekly Sabbath. The card at Romans 14 gives what the churches teach.

Paul says it is good not to drink wine if it makes a brother stumble. He does not forbid wine; the context is the weak person's scruple, possibly over wine poured out to idols or the Jewish habit of avoiding Gentile wine (Daniel 1:8). The Bible's other statements on wine, from blessing to warning, are on this topic page.

"The kingdom of God is not food and drink. It is righteousness, peace and joy in the Holy Spirit." Paul uses the phrase seldom, and here he defines it by what the Spirit gives, not by rules or practices. The picture is of a kingdom already present in the life of the church, one in which disputes over food are out of place.

Paul says that believers submit to rulers "for the sake of conscience" (13:5), and in chapter 14 he deals with the consciences of the strong and the weak: each should be "fully sure in their own mind" (14:5); "anything not done out of faith is sin" (14:23), the sense being that to act against one's own conviction is wrong even if the act would otherwise be fine. Conscience is never a final judge, because only the Lord judges (14:4, 10).

Paul commends Phoebe, a "servant" (diakonos) of the church in Cenchreae and a patron of many (16:1-2); he names Prisca before her husband Aquila, a coworker (16:3); he greets Junia, "outstanding among the apostles" (16:7), and Mary, Tryphaena, Tryphosa and Persis, who "toil" or "toiled" in the Lord (16:6, 12). The early church fathers took Junia as a woman and an apostle; the male name "Junias" appears much later. Churches today draw different conclusions about ordination, as the card at 16:7 shows.

Phoebe is called a diakonos of the church in Cenchreae, a word that means "servant" and also names the office of deacon (Philippians 1:1; 1 Timothy 3:8-13). Many commentators think Paul names a recognized role. Origen took the verse to show that women were set in the ministry of the church. The word "deaconess" came later.

Paul calls them his "fellow workers in Christ Jesus" who "risked their own necks" for his life, and greets the church that meets in their house. They had been expelled from Rome under Claudius (Acts 18:2), worked with Paul in Corinth and Ephesus (Acts 18:18-26; 1 Corinthians 16:19), and by the time of Romans were back in Rome. Paul names Prisca first, as Luke does in four of the six places where both appear.

The greetings of 16:21-23 come from people at Corinth: Timothy, Lucius, Jason, Sosipater, Gaius (host of the whole church), Erastus (the city treasurer) and Quartus. Phoebe came from Cenchreae, the port of Corinth (16:1). Paul had been there three months in the winter before his last visit to Jerusalem (Acts 20:2-3). The Erastus inscription at Corinth and the judgment seat in the forum (14:10; Acts 18:12) are physical traces of his setting.

sections.h: The collection for the poor in Jerusalem (Romans 15:25-31)
sections.b: Paul tells the Romans that Macedonia and Achaia chose gladly to pool a gift for the poor among the saints in Jerusalem, and that the Gentiles, having shared in their spiritual blessings, owe them material help. He asks for prayer for the trip. He had agreed years earlier to "remember the poor" (Galatians 2:10). Acts mentions the gift only in passing (Acts 24:17).

sections.h: Christ the servant of the circumcised (Romans 15:8-12)
sections.b: In the closing section of his argument, Paul says Christ became a servant of the circumcised "to show God's truth, by making firm the promises made to the fathers," and that the Gentiles then give glory to God for mercy. A chain of four quotations shows Jews and Gentiles praising God together. The Gentile debt to Jerusalem (15:27) is the same picture in money. These verses are used against the idea that the church replaced Israel.

sections.h: The root of Jesse and Christ's example (Romans 15)
sections.b: Paul hears the Messiah speaking in the Psalms ("The insults of those who insult you fell on me," Psalm 69:9, in Romans 15:3; Psalm 18:49 in Romans 15:9) and ends with Isaiah 11:10, the "root of Jesse," who rises to rule the Gentiles. The Davidic Messiah is also the servant of the circumcised (15:8).

Paul says he does "a priest's work for the good news of God" so that the Gentiles may become "an offering God welcomes, made holy by the Holy Spirit." He was not a priest by descent; the language is a picture of his preaching. It echoes Isaiah 66:20, where the nations bring back the exiles as an offering.

"The God of peace will crush Satan under your feet, and soon." It is the only mention of Satan in Romans and may echo God's words to the serpent in Genesis 3:15. The believers' feet are the instrument; God does the crushing.

Paul writes that salvation is nearer than when they first believed and that the day is close. The nearness has been read as an expected return in his lifetime or as a nearness that is always true. The Roman and Anglican churches read these verses on the first Sunday of Advent.

"Keep no debt hanging over anyone, except the debt of loving one another." Most commentators read it as "pay what you owe," since the law allows loans. Some Christian groups have read it as a ban on all borrowing. The word "owe" returns in 15:27, where the Gentiles owe Jerusalem a material gift.

Behind the worries of the weak lay the problem of meat and wine that had been offered to idols (compare 1 Corinthians 8 and 10). Paul never mentions idols in Romans 14, but the practices of vegetables and water echo Jews in Gentile settings (Daniel 1; Tobit 1:10-11).

Paul describes the believer's relation to the Lord in the language of slavery: "Be slaves of the Lord" (12:11), and the household slave who belongs to another master (14:4). The point is who owns the person, not a defense of the institution.

Paul is about to go to Jerusalem with the collection, and he asks the Romans to pray that he may be rescued from those in Judea who refuse to believe and that his service may be acceptable to the saints. Acts shows what happened: a welcome from the brothers, a vow in the temple, and arrest (Acts 21:17-36).

The end of Romans is the fullest picture of Paul's circle: he has finished his work from Jerusalem to Illyricum, plans Spain, and sends greetings from Timothy, Lucius, Jason, Sosipater, Tertius (who wrote the letter), Gaius, Erastus and Quartus. He greets more than two dozen people he knows in Rome.
The collection that Paul describes in Romans 15:25-28 is the largest gift project of the New Testament. Acts 24:17 calls it "alms for my people."
